item.title: Optimization, From the Locker Room to the Boardroom
item.description:
Burnout

Optimization, From the Locker Room to the Boardroom

What elite athletes know about performance optimization that executives don't.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Business loves a great sports analogy but misses out on sport's most important lessons.
  • Optimized, elite performance requires periodized rest. Without it, chronic stress onset becomes inevitable.
  • Mistaking performance optimization for wellness can worsen burnout.
  • The wellness economy has now hit $6.8 trillion, yet burnout continues to rise.
Source: KeithJJ/Pixabay

I am a sucker for a great sports analogy. In fact, my PhD thesis was literally titled From the Locker Room to the Boardroom, and to this day, Al Pacino's epic 'Game of Inches' speech from Any Given Sunday (delivered by fictional coach Tony D'Amato) remains a fixture in my eMBA lectures.

Historically, the business world has always loved a great sports anecdote, but this interest has accelerated in recent years, with the explicit adoption of performance optimization trends (sleep trackers, ice baths, heart rate monitoring) routinely used by competitive athletes. The data stacks up. 82% of consumers in the US, UK, and China already rank wellness as a top personal priority (McKinsey, 2024). Meanwhile, the global wellness economy has just hit a record $6.8 trillion (Global Wellness Institute, 2025), on track to reach $9.8 trillion by 2029, while financial titans like SoftBank and Bank of America now release their own wellness and burnout studies.

Are we performing more like athletes as a result?

No.

In fact, around two-thirds of employees globally are now reporting burnout (Forbes, 2025), with Gallup estimating that disengagement and burnout are draining the world economy of an estimated $8.8 trillion in lost productivity every year (Gallup, 2024). The reason, it turns out, is that most corporate wellness interventions are built on a fundamental misdiagnosis—the mistaken belief that burnout is caused by a lack of individual resilience, rather than a systemic failure to manage workplace demands (American Institute of Stress, 2023). Treat the wrong problem, and you get the wrong result.

Here's the deeper issue, one that you can tackle immediately: Performance optimization is not wellness; in fact, the two are completely separate concepts. Mistaking one for the other, as it turns out, can be intensely problematic.

HRV and data analytics image
Source: RDNE Stock Project / Pixabay

The Optimization Trap

Meet Jackson. Vice president at a large investment bank, he's recently been battling broken sleep and falling energy levels. His response is a characteristically proactive one—the deployment of a performance optimization stack (a sleep tracker monitoring HRV and deep-sleep percentages, morning cold plunges, and ramped-up gym sessions). On paper, he looks like a model of science-backed wellness.

In practice, he feels worse.

Jackson's mistake is one of the most common in executive performance: Like an athlete, he has to perform, but unlike an athlete, he has no periodization built into his diary. Periodization is the systematic cycling of training load, intensity, and recovery. All athletes know that periodized stages of rest are an absolute necessity, crucial for elite performance to occur. Subsequently, Jackson's allostatic load—the cumulative physiological 'wear and tear' that chronic stress exacts on the body (McEwen, 1998)—has already crossed a threshold. Adding further physiological demands at this stage doesn't build resilience; it compounds the problem.

Compounding this, his sleep tracker may be contributing to a condition researchers at Rush University Medical Center have termed orthosomnia, a paradoxical anxiety about achieving perfect sleep metrics that, through elevated allostatic load, actively disrupts the sleep it is meant to improve (Baron et al., 2017).

Periodization Matters

Periodization is one of the most robustly evidenced principles in sports science (Issurin, 2010). The physiological adaptations that support peak performance do not occur during training stress; they occur in the recovery window that follows. Remove that window, and you are more likely to see symptoms similar to overtraining and burnout: persistent fatigue, sleep disturbance, impaired cognitive function, mood dysregulation, and suppressed immune response (Meeusen et al., 2013; Kreher & Schwartz, 2012)—burnout staples we are seeing more of in the corporate world.

Wrong Stage, Wrong Strategy

The deeper structural problem is that business culture (unlike sport) has no shared framework for distinguishing between a system primed for optimization and one that urgently needs recovery.

In sport a coach reads an athlete's HRV trends, subjective fatigue scores, and training load data then critically adjusts the program accordingly. In the boardroom, those same signals—disrupted sleep quality (even before sleep duration shortens), declining HRV, irritability, emerging cynicism, reduced motivation for previously enjoyable activities (Åkerstedt, 2006; Maslach & Leiter, 2016)—are routinely ignored, or worse, treated as evidence that more effort is needed.

The physiological reality is unambiguous: When our sympathetic nervous system's 'fight-or-flight' drive begins to outpace parasympathetic 'rest-and-digest' recovery and allostatic load accumulates, performance optimization strategies become physiologically counterproductive (McEwen, 2007), accelerating the very chronic stress they were designed to address. In short, you cannot push or optimize your way out of a stress-response deficit. What you need is recovery.

Work colleagues walking outdoors during a break
Source: Mizuno K / Pixabay

The good news is that meaningful recovery does not require weeks off the grid. Research consistently shows that daily, short breaks for low-stimulation micro-recovery can produce measurable physiological benefit. Just a few minutes of slow, diaphragmatic breathing, for example, has been shown to increase parasympathetic activity (Bentley et al., 2023), while a brief exposure to nature—even sitting near a window with a view of greenery!—measurably reduces cortisol and accelerates autonomic recovery (Twohig-Bennett & Jones, 2018). The common thread is low stimulation: The nervous system recovers when demand is temporarily and genuinely removed.

The earlier emerging stress signals are identified and addressed, the greater the leverage for recovery and redirection (Karakolias, 2025), so any winning performance approach means prioritizing wellness recovery when you need it, before performance optimization is even on the table.

To paraphrase Coach D'Amato, the inches we need are everywhere around us. But here's the uncomfortable truth: Taking an unscheduled afternoon off, leaving the laptop closed over the weekend, or simply going to bed an hour earlier will never generate the LinkedIn engagement of a 5am ice bath or a new HRV personal best. Recovery is unglamorous. It doesn't photograph well. And yet it is precisely what the science, and every serious athletic program on the planet, tells us is the non-negotiable foundation of peak performance.

item.title: The Mental Health of a Knicks Championship With No Sequel
item.description:
Sport and Competition

The Mental Health of a Knicks Championship With No Sequel

Why winning once and walking away can be healthier than chasing a dynasty.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • The Knicks won their first title since 1973, and freedom from repeat expectations is a mental health gift.
  • Like the 2011 Mavericks, this team can savor greatness without the dynasty pressure haunting favored rosters.
  • With no sequel demanded, the Knicks escape anticipatory anxiety and arrival fallacy that weighs on contenders.

On Saturday night in San Antonio, the New York Knicks did what they had done all postseason. They fell behind early, then rallied from 16 points down to win Game 5 by 94-90 and close out the series 4-1. It was the franchise's first title since 1973. Jalen Brunson poured in 45 points and walked off as the unanimous Finals MVP.

I have spent years watching what happens to people after the final whistle and after the final exam. The celebration is real. The quiet that follows is real too. What keeps pulling at me with this Knicks team is something the confetti tends to hide. This group may have won the healthiest kind of championship there is, the kind that arrives with no demand for a sequel.

To see why, rewind to 2011. Dirk Nowitzki and the Dallas Mavericks beat a Miami Heat team built around LeBron James, Dwyane Wade, and Chris Bosh, a roster assembled to win for years. The Mavericks won that title and then faded from contention. Dirk, the heart of that team, never returned to the Finals. Fifteen years later, that championship is remembered fondly, and no one files it under failure for never repeating, because no one expected a repeat in the first place.

The Psychology Behind Expectation and Happiness in Sports

That absence of expectation is a gift, and psychology explains why. Researchers describe the arrival fallacy, the belief that reaching a goal will deliver lasting contentment, and the hedonic treadmill, our habit of resetting to baseline and immediately craving the next high. Dynasties live on that treadmill. The instant a favored team wins, the only question left is whether they can do it again. The prize for greatness becomes a heavier load of expectation.

Part of what makes this Knicks title feel so settled is the way it was built. Brunson is the engine, but the supporting cast tells the story of a team assembled to win now rather than to reign for a decade. These are players in their primes, brought together at the right moment, and that matters psychologically as much as it does competitively. A roster built for a single shining window invites everyone, players and fans alike, to treat the window itself as the achievement. There is no five-year plan hanging over this team. There is only this, and this is already enough.

The Knicks now stand apart from the teams chasing them. The Spurs are young and built through the draft, with Victor Wembanyama anchoring what many already call a coming dynasty. The Oklahoma City Thunder carry that same weight with MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and general/genius manager Sam Presti. The Lakers and Celtics live under championship expectation every season as a matter of identity. Those franchises will measure each year against a standard that only a title can satisfy. The Knicks reached the summit, and the next climb will not begin with the same urgency.

There is freedom in that position. Positive psychology uses the term savoring for our ability to fully attend to and stretch out a good experience. Savoring gets harder when the mind is already sprinting toward the next obligation. A team expected to repeat cannot savor for long, because its offseason turns into a countdown. The Knicks can savor this for decades. Their place in history is crystallized, and the meaning of this run is settled no matter what next season brings.

The Role of Anticipatory Anxiety and the Release from Expectation

Anticipatory anxiety, the worry we feel about events that have not happened yet, feeds on high stakes and high expectations. Remove the expectation and the anxiety loses its fuel. Knicks fans woke up on Sunday with a championship and no verdict hanging over next June. For a fan base, and for the players, that is a rare and generous psychological place to stand.

I have watched this play out on a smaller scale on the sidelines and in the classroom. The athletes and students who struggle most are often the ones carrying a past success they feel obligated to reproduce. A young player who has one brilliant game starts to press and tighten, performing for an audience made of his own highlights. The ones who compete freely tend to treat each moment as complete in itself. Achievement turns heavy the moment we sign a contract with ourselves that says we have to do it again.

Here is the detail I find most freeing: this title came 53 years after the last one, and very few people would be shocked if the next Knicks championship arrived another half century from now. That might sound like a grim forecast. I write it as a liberating one. It means this team gets to live outside the brutal accounting that haunts dynasties. They will not be branded frauds for losing in the second round next spring. They get to be champions, fully and finally, with the verdict already entered.

The Difficulty of Repeating as Champions

Consider that the league has now produced eight different champions in eight years, the longest such streak in its history. Repeating has rarely been harder. The Knicks did the hard part once, and the math of the modern NBA quietly gives them permission to stop there.

The healthiest goals in life are often the ones we can finish and then release. We see it at graduations, in completed manuscripts, in a single great season that never has to become a career. The hunt for permanence can quietly rob us of the joy of what we already earned. The Knicks chased one thing for 53 years, they caught it, and now they get to hold it without being told to catch it again next year. For a franchise, for a city, and for anyone who has ever felt trapped by their own success, that may be the real lesson of this title. Some forms of greatness are a destination, reached once and kept forever.

item.title: How to Help Young Athletes Avoid a Narrow Sense of Self
item.description:
Sport and Competition

How to Help Young Athletes Avoid a Narrow Sense of Self

How coaches and parents can foster multidimensional growth.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Many athletes struggle when their sports career stalls or ends, not knowing what to do moving forward.
  • Problems associated with an end to sports can be prevented by helping athletes discover other valued things.
  • Parents and coaches need to project a perspective that there's more to a meaningful life than just sports.
Source: AI Generated (Gemini)

You’re far more than an athlete.

That’s a message I deliver to athletes of all ages, especially the young ones, many of whom end up suffering due to a life definition revolving almost exclusively around sports. They often implode when something goes wrong in their athletic endeavors, as detailed in a previous post.

That over-reliance on sports for self-value creates enormous pressure, stunts performance effectiveness, and kills the joy of athletic participation.

More importantly, it can create a void of purpose and direction when they can no longer play like they used to, due to being a non-starter, an injury, or because their sports career completely ends. These circumstances often result in a bottomless pit of meaninglessness and sadness. Such athletes lack—and are in dire need of—a multidimensional sense of self.

The purpose of this post is to encourage coaches and parents to help young people understand that there’s much more to life than just sports. Young people can balance their lives by identifying other important, often hidden, dimensions of their lives.

Promoting Full Meaning

The first step a psychologist can take to encourage people to discover their true meaning is to have them identify what they deeply value. That’s a cornerstone of Acceptance and Commitment Training (ACT), a popular approach to clinical and sports psychology around the world.

Paraphrasing ACT creator Stephen Hayes: What a person deeply values gives them a unique life meaning and guides purposeful behavior. Those elements of value include the people who are important to them and the virtues they want to embody, such as kindness, honesty, humility, etc. Clients are asked to record the people and virtues they value most.

Going beyond ACT and borrowing from Stephen A. Covey’s 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, they are then asked to identify four to seven key roles they play in life. Those may include things like son, student, friend, and of course, athlete. Once the roles have been identified, clients are asked to briefly write how each role is to be played.

Following Covey’s guidelines, clients then create a mission statement or mantra incorporating the people, values, and roles they identified. They are encouraged to create it in a personalized way to serve as a motivating reminder of who they are and what truly matters to them. It’s a creation they can revise as they see fit to recapture their continuously evolving self.

Next, each person is encouraged to review their values, roles, and mission statements regularly to remind them of who they are and that they are far more than just an athlete.

Finally, athletes are asked to live the values, roles, and mission statement they identified and composed, via what ACT terms committed action, making what they wrote come to life with their chosen behavior.

For Coaches and Parents

Please stop making sports the be-all, end-all of a young person’s existence. Encourage them to reflect on the rest of their life and what they will do with their future beyond athletics.

Quit making a sport or team a forced, year-around commitment. Give kids time between seasons to play other sports or engage with other things they choose. Keep in mind: The NFL gives players a seven-month break from team practice (with a few mini-camps sprinkled in) after the season ends in January. There are also no team practices in Major League Baseball between the end of the season in October through the beginning of spring training in late February.

It makes no sense that kids between the ages of 12 and 18 are expected and coerced to practice more than professional athletes. That’s what’s happening in today’s crazed youth sport culture. Is it any wonder that young athletes grow up with such limited meaning and direction for their lives?

Empower the independence of young people, as emphasized by Jonathon Haidt in his groundbreaking book, The Anxious Generation. Let kids decide what they do during a sport's off-season. Allowing the athlete to choose when they practice, minus the forced coercion of a coach or parent, enables more productive training and better well-being.

Obviously, athletes must comply with team and coach expectations during the season, but even within that timeframe, coaches and parents need to recognize when enough is enough. Kids have school, family, friends, and other roles and obligations they desire to fulfill. Too much forced time devoted to sports can lead to burnout as well as an all-too narrow sense of self.

item.title: Beware of Frankensteining in a Relationship
item.description:
Mating

Beware of Frankensteining in a Relationship

How to tell if you are Frankensteining in a relationship, or getting Frankensteined.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Frankensteining is one-sidedly trying to change your partner into what you would like them to be.
  • It can be conscious or unconscious. You can even convince yourself that you are simply being supportive
  • Frankensteining can be a sign that you are with the wrong person or are trying to control your partner.
  • Recognize Frankensteining as soon as possible and then have a frank, open talk with your partner about it.
Frankensteining is one-sidedly trying to change your partner into what you would like him or her to be.
Source: Daisy Anderson from Pexels

Typically, you don't want your partner to be a monster, but...welcome to Frankensteining. It's a new trending-on-social-media term to describe a longtime phenomenon in dating and relationships. It's when you one-sidedly try to change your partner into something that he or she is not, based simply on who and what you would like your partner to be.

Frankensteining Comes from the Frankenstein Stories

The term comes from Dr. Frankenstein, the mad scientist who created a monster from assembled parts in Mary Shelley's 1818 novel. Frankenstein and his monster subsequently starred in a slew of movies, nearly all of which were not exactly rom-coms. In the 1931 film Frankenstein, the monster didn't turn out to be what Dr. Frankenstein wanted. The monster ended up going on a rampage, killing a bunch of people before being trapped by the villagers in a windmill, which the villagers then set afire, burning the monster alive or perhaps a-dead. That's typically not what you want to happen in a relationship.

What is Frankensteining?

Frankensteining is when you try to morph the appearance, interests, habits, behavior, or personality of someone you are dating or have some kind of romantic relationship with into what you would prefer. Usually, this is toward what you envision to be your "ideal" partner. You might try to convince them to switch to a job or career that you prefer and not the one that they necessarily want. Or you might get your partner to re-do his or her wardrobe, hairstyle, make-up or even body parts through plastic surgery.

Frankensteining Can Be Unconscious

You could do this intentionally. You may look at your partner and think, "Nuh uh, not going to do this," and consciously try to re-make him or her into something different. This could be a wholesale all-at-once change, My Fair Lady style, or piece-by-piece over time. You might even have a multi-year Project 2029 plan so that by the summer of 2029, you will have Margot Robbie or someone from BTS as a partner.

Often, though, Frankensteining is unconscious. You could be thinking that you are simply being supportive, just trying to help your partner be a better person. You could even convince yourself that it's what your partner deep down really wants. Frankesteining could start with a small thing that doesn't significantly change your partner, like a single wardrobe accessory change or a soft pivot to eating fruitcake on Sundays. But slowly and steadily, things could escalate toward bigger and bigger changes.

How to Distinguish Frankensteining From Support

The key distinction in Frankensteining is that deep down you are thinking "If only my partner were different in [fill in your favorite things] way, everything would be so, so much better." And that "different" is significantly different from who your partner really is. It's one thing to help bring out your partner's true self and your partner achieve what he or she really wants. It's something totally different to disregard your partner's wishes.

Therefore, you've got to ask yourself whether you are with your partner because you truly like him or her—the real him or her. Or whether you are with your partner simply because you couldn't get a better fit for you. The latter is awful for your partner and not good for your either. Dating is about finding the right fit for each other, and not potentially-the-right-fit-if-all-of-these-things-eventually-change.

Why Might You Frankenstein Someone

Ask yourself whether you really like your partner for who he or she already is truly.
Source: Chris Luengas from Pexels

You can end up Frankensteining someone when you latch onto that person for particular characteristics such as "Oh, he is so good-looking" or "She actually has a job and can pay for stuff" or "That person has a pulse and actually likes me" but are not really fond of the complete package. Frankensteining is a big risk when you date someone simply because you are lonely, desperate, or. both. For example, I was once Frankensteined by a woman who was really in love with her best friend but he didn't reciprocate. Guess who she tried to morph me into.

Frankensteining can be about control, too. You may be thinking, "Great, now I have a gigantic Ken or Barbie doll at my command." And that doll can essentially go as the following lyrics from that "Barbie Girl" song go: "Make me walk, make me talk, do whatever you please. I can act like a star, I can beg on my knees." Again, most partners wouldn't want to be such a doll for you. Life in such plastic is not fantastic.

What to Do if You Are Frankensteining

It's important to recognize when you might be Frankensteining, why, and to what degree. If you do indeed love most of who your partner really is and just want to make some adjustments, maybe have a frank conversation with them to see if they agree. But realize that life and relationships are not perfect. And ask yourself whether such changes would really matter.

If, on the other hand, the changes you want to make are rather significant, then maybe you are not with the right person. In such a case, it may be better for you and your partner to go your separate ways rather than continue to waste each other's time. This can allow both of you the opportunity to find your true matches.

What to Do if You Are Being Frankensteined

Of course, if you are the one getting Frankensteined, it's important to sit bolt upright and have a frank talk with your partner—unless you are OK with being Frankenstein's monster. Ask you partner whether they like you for who you are. If the answer is anything besides a firm "Yes," then maybe it's time to leave the relationship and head to the village.

Ultimately, it's better to recognize any Frankensteining in either direction as soon as possible. Because no one should be stuck in such a monstrous situation.

item.title: The Imagination Network Is Not the Villain
item.description:
Imagination

The Imagination Network Is Not the Villain

What mindfulness researchers get wrong about the imagination network.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • The default mode network—the brain's Imagination Network—drives memory, empathy, and creativity.
  • Rumination isn't mind-wandering: a ruminating mind is locked in one groove, not roaming free.
  • Whether mind-wandering helps or hurts depends on its content and type, not the wandering itself.
Source: Donald Merrill/Unsplash

“A wandering mind is an unhappy mind,” declared Killingsworth & Gilbert.

And reader, to borrow a phrase from Michael Jordan: I took it personally.

I’m a creativity researcher who has spent years studying the upside of the wandering mind—positive-constructive daydreaming: the playful, future-oriented inner life that fuels imagination and insight. And Jerome L. Singer, the “father of daydreaming” who pioneered that whole line of work, became a close personal friend and sat on my dissertation committee. He is, I’m quite sure, rolling in his grave every time he hears a mindfulness researcher hate on the cognitive machinery behind daydreaming.

They’ve got the wrong villain.

Meet the accused

The “default mode network” is the system that’s most active when you turn inward—when you stop chasing an external goal and start to drift, remember, imagine, reflect, and wonder. I’ve spent my career arguing the exact opposite, which is why I call it the Imagination Network: because what it’s doing is anything but nothing!

Here’s the résumé of the accused:

  • It writes your story. It builds your autobiographical memory—the running internal narrative that makes you you across time.
  • It travels through time. It lets you imagine your future self, rehearse your goals, and run the “what if” scenarios that planning a life requires.
  • It reads other minds. It’s the seat of perspective-taking, empathy, and theory of mind.
  • It incubates your best ideas—and powers creative flow.

These are not idle defaults or bugs to be patched out. They are the soul of human existence! They are, in the most literal sense, essential to self-actualization itself.

And here’s the part the mindfulness researchers keep missing: the network they smear as the self-absorbed “me” network is also the “us” network. It’s how we connect—and how we love.

That is not the résumé of a villain. That’s the résumé of the most human part of the human brain.

The real culprit was never the network

So why does the network keep showing up at the scene of every crime? Because it also hosts rumination—the stuck, self-attacking loop where the same dark thought circles the drain.

But here’s the irony: rumination isn’t even really wandering. When you ruminate, your mind isn’t roaming free—it’s locked in, grinding one groove.

“A wandering mind is an unhappy mind” turned out to be far more nuanced than the title promised: whether mind-wandering lifts or sinks your mood depends on its content and type. Spontaneous, negative, can’t-stop-it wandering hurts. Deliberate, prospective, playful wandering helps.

The crime isn’t wandering. It’s getting trapped in your wanderings, and losing the freedom to wander back out.

The irony that gives the whole thing away

I find it rather amusing that the people prosecuting the Imagination Network keep, in the same breath, marveling at its gifts.

For most of Michael Pollan's book How to Change Your Mind, the default mode network is presented as the ego to be vanquished. In his final chapter, he closes with a triumphant coda titled “Going to Meet My Default Mode Network,” in which he straps on a 128-electrode cap in Judson Brewer’s lab to drive down activity in his posterior cingulate cortex—a major hub of the Imagination Network. The whole arc of the book seems to point to this defining moment where he considers the whole journey a success because he silenced his Imagination Network.

This is really strange because then in the epilogue of the book he ends in rapture over a mental space that keeps handing him “usable ideas, images, or metaphors”—“one of the great gifts” of the journey. Folks: that’s positive-constructive daydreaming. That’s the Imagination Network. He demonizes it for nearly 400 pages, then ends his book in awe of it.

A strong sense of self is a very different thing than a strong ego. You can have a quiet ego and maintain a strong sense of who you are, what you value, and who you wish to become.

You don’t have to dissolve the imagination to be free. You have to free it.

To be fair to the prosecution

I’m not here to tell you meditation doesn’t work. I’m a regular mindfulness meditation practitioner myself. I did the full eight-week Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction course and came away genuinely changed. The benefits are real, and meditation is excellent training for the executive attention network. But the single deepest thing I learned on the cushion is the very point of this essay: mindfulness is not the opposite of mind-wandering.

A regular meditation practice doesn’t delete the imagination network; it tunes it, calming the self-critical, ruminative parts while leaving the imaginative ones free to roam. Regulation isn’t suppression—it’s the freedom to choose when to focus and when to wander.

It’s the integration, not the war

My colleagues and I have been showing that creative cognition requires a strong integration between the executive attention network and the Imagination Network. The receipts, if you want them: default–executive coupling supports creative idea production; openness to experience and default-network efficiency; how eminent and non-eminent thinkers differ during creative thought; brain morphometry and creative achievement; and Roger Beaty’s recent work showing that “control-default hubs” act as an integrative core for complex cognition and creativity.

In our work, the Imagination Network isn’t the villain. It’s the hero.

And I suspect that’s the real reason the default mode network keeps getting cast as the enemy. Underneath the neuroscience sits an older ideology—that the self is the problem, and the destination is no self at all.

But run that program to completion and you don’t get a sage. You get a freaking zombie! No inner life, no rich imagination, no thoughts of the future, no contact with your own deepest memories, and no self left to actualize. Who, exactly, wants that? The whole game is the two networks working together—and keeping the strong sense of self.

A different goal

The aim of a life well-lived is not a quiet mind. It’s a free one—a mind that can drop fully into the present when the present is what’s called for, and roam the past, the future, and the wildly possible when that’s what’s called for, and move flexibly between the two.

So no—I won’t be “defeating” my default mode network. I’ll keep it, thank you very much! The rumination I’ll work on. The imagination I’m keeping for good.

The Imagination Network isn’t the villain of your inner life. It’s the protagonist.

item.title: How to Talk to Patients About Their AI Use
item.description:
Therapy

How to Talk to Patients About Their AI Use

Knowing the right questions to ask can turn curiosity into useful assessment.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Patients are using AI for emotional support, advice, and mental health, often without telling clinicians.
  • AI chatbots may reinforce specific vulnerabilities in OCD, eating disorders, and depression.
  • AI literacy is becoming an essential part of clinical practice, and practical training can help clinicians.

Co-authored by Jill Noorily at the Division of Digital Psychiatry at BIDMC.

This post is part 1 of a series.

A man you have been seeing for several months for OCD and anxiety comes into his next session saying he stopped attending the weekly support groups he had previously found helpful. Upon further discussion, he discloses that he has been spending several hours each night talking to an AI chatbot, saying, "It understands me better than anyone."

As his clinician, how would you respond?

Our team at the Division of Digital Psychiatry sent a similar pre-screening vignette and question above to over 100 mental health clinicians to better understand how clinicians currently approach these conversations.

Most clinicians first approached the scenario with curiosity, but their curiosity lacked a target of inquiry. This vignette presents the clinician with three clinical facts: a dose (several hours each night), a feeling (it understands them better than anyone), and a functional cost (they have abandoned a support group that was helping). Many clinicians missed fundamental inquiries that explore the dose and use pattern. So, while clinical curiosity was present, there wasn't a clear sense of how to harness it.

Clinicians need to know which questions can help distinguish benign AI use from concerning use, and which questions to ask to explore patient use. They also need a technical understanding of the tools to understand engagement risk.

This is a teachable gap in clinical understanding.

A Therapist's Practical Assessment Framework for Patient AI Use

To address this gap, the Division of Digital Psychiatry and the Society of Digital Psychiatry are hosting a learning collaborative for clinicians to talk about how AI has entered their patients' lives. The group consists of over a dozen psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, digital navigators, and therapists spanning six continents and working with a variety of different clinical populations. The goal of these conversations is to equip participants with tools and information to have informed conversations with patients who are already engaging with these technologies.

Throughout our collaborative sessions, we have developed a practical assessment framework. When a patient discloses AI chatbot use, clinicians should be curious about:

  • Dose and pattern: How often? For how long? At what times of day or night?
  • Content: What do you talk about? Do you find yourself returning to the same topics?
  • Function: What do you get from it? What does it feel like afterward?
  • Substitution: Is this replacing something? Is it reducing previously helpful coping strategies like group therapy, personal connections?
  • The chatbot itself: Which one? Would you be willing to share the conversation transcript?

Something the group has discussed is that patients don't often naturally disclose their use to clinicians. Mental health already carries stigma, and many patients are used to keeping their behaviors private. For these reasons, clinicians need to be proactive in engaging patients about their AI use.

Risks of AI Use for Different Mental Health Conditions

The learning collaborative also discussed ways AI might interact with different mental health conditions. An AI interaction that one person finds helpful or benign might be risky for another person who brings different mental health vulnerabilities to the conversation. At this point, chatbots don't have the metacognition or understanding of the psychiatric condition the user might be dealing with.

This is why clinicians need more than a general awareness that "AI can make mistakes" or "AI can be sycophantic." Instead, they need to understand how the structural tendencies of LLMs can play into the specific vulnerabilities of a given pathology.

Some examples that the group spoke about:

  • OCD: Seeking reassurance from chatbots can help people reduce anxiety about obsessions in the moment, but often it can strengthen the reassurance-seeking cycle over time. From the perspective of an OCD patient, a chatbot can become a tool that feeds the OCD cycle of behavior.
  • Eating Disorders: Patients might ask chatbots about what they ate, how they look, or whether certain behaviors are "ok." Because LLMs tend to be affirming, they may fail to challenge distorted beliefs. The lack of pushback might inadvertently lead to unsafe situations for users with eating disorders.
  • Depression and Rumination: Depressive rumination involves returning to the same negative thoughts and feelings repeatedly. Chatbots are designed to continue conversations, so they will support rumination and possibly reinforce those thinking patterns.
  • Social Avoidance: Patients who struggle socially might be prone to using chatbots as a replacement for human connection, deepening social withdrawal. This might lead people to isolate themselves from their community or resources for help.
  • Mania, Psychosis, or Delusional Thinking: Chatbots can elaborate and continue a line of reasoning without recognizing when it might be deepening unreal thinking. This could lead a patient further into maladaptive beliefs.

To have meaningful conversations, this group had to remain small. Interest exceeded the program's capacity, revealing an unmet need among clinicians seeking practical guidance. Although only one cohort could participate in the pilot, the program's structure offers a model that other clinical teams can adapt as they develop future training opportunities.

Recognizing an unmet need for clinicians to access training, the team at the Division of Digital Psychiatry created a free interactive training on how to approach patients' AI use. It introduces clinicians to six practical areas: literacy, risks, recognition, documentation, response, and output. Participants learn how large language models function, why certain structural features create predictable vulnerabilities, how to recognize patterns of use that may warrant further assessment, how to document AI-related factors when they alter the clinical picture, and how to respond thoughtfully when patients disclose concerning experiences.

One of the greatest risks surrounding AI in mental healthcare may be clinician unpreparedness. Patients deserve clinicians who can approach these conversations with curiosity, humility, and enough knowledge to ask better questions and distinguish between use that appears helpful, use that deserves monitoring, and use that calls for intervention.

AI has become part of many patients' lives. Learning how to talk about it has become just another part of good clinical care.

item.title: Which Acts of Giving Make Us Happier?
item.description:
Altruism

Which Acts of Giving Make Us Happier?

Some aspects of giving are more linked to positivity than others.

Posted June 14, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that doing good deeds for others elevates the giver's well-being.
  • Extra effort—doing more than expected—leads to greater feelings of positivity.
  • Helping certain people doesn't impact happiness; the act of giving itself matters more.
Source: Gustavo Fring/Pexels

There’s a video I love to show one of my classes. It highlights people doing something nice for others in quick succession, with someone doing a good deed for another, followed by that person paying it forward and helping another individual. I think students appreciate it, and it never gets old for me. I smile—inside and outside—every time.

When we engage in acts of goodness like this, research shows we enjoy more well-being. But how does that occur? Does it matter what we do? What about whom we’re doing it for or how they respond?

How Different Good Deeds Affect the Giver

Researchers looked at these questions in a recent exploratory study; it was intended to see what connections exist rather than examine any set hypotheses. They found that some facets of thoughtful actions were linked to people feeling even more upbeat, while others weren’t.

First, let’s talk in terms of what people do for others: Folks who offered an object or money seemed to experience more of a mood boost compared to other things, like offering time or sharing expertise.

There are two important points to park on here. First, the researchers noted that even though these two forms of giving seemed the most connected to positivity, giving to people overall was linked to feeling brighter; so other actions can still leave us feeling more content. Second, the paper's examples of the money and objects people gave weren’t lavish. They involved things like adding more to a tip or giving someone coffee.

More significantly, greater cheerfulness was related to doing more than what would be typical in that situation. Let’s say your friend asked if you’d be willing to pick something up from the grocery store for them on your way over. In addition to doing what they asked you to do, you also stop off and pick up a coffee for them. That additional step goes past what the situation called for.

How the Recipient’s Reaction Shapes the Giver's Happiness

The results also showed that the recipient's reaction is related to a bigger mood boost. We seem to feel more content when the person we helped shows appreciation.

We also may feel happier when we give to different people in diverse ways. In other words, if we shift how we do it, we appear to feel more content than if we don’t revise what we’re doing. However, who we’re giving to doesn’t seem to make a difference in the happiness enhancement we get, nor does it matter if the good deed directly helps both another person and ourselves, or just that individual.

Again, this study is in the exploratory stage, so we should consider the results with some caution. That said, it's still worth being curious and paying attention to how we feel when we do good deeds. What aspects of it might make more of a difference in how you feel?
